title: Should natural lifters bulk / cut?
summary: He argues bulk/cut cycles come from enhanced bodybuilding and don't suit most naturals, who lose much of the muscle gained when they cut. Only the very skinny should bulk and the very fat should cut; everyone else should hover near maintenance with a small surplus (a 'perma-bulk'), since yo-yo dieting wastes energy that should go into training.

claims.claim: He says he is fairly new to diet work so won't give precise dietary guidance, but has a lot of experience with bulking.
Bulking and cutting stem from enhanced bodybuilders, who can keep adding muscle however much fat they gain and keep most muscle while cutting with drugs.
A natural who gains a lot of weight fast will lose much of the muscle gained when cutting, and didn't gain much muscle in the first place.
Unpopular opinion: natural lifters generally shouldn't bulk or cut; only extremes should: very skinny people should bulk and very fat people should cut.

Skinny lifters can gain muscle without a big weight gain and heavier lifters can gain muscle while slowly losing weight, but in practice focusing purely on reaching the weight goal fast is more realistic.
Trying to chase strength goals during weight loss can sabotage a diet: people losing weight feel weak, lifts drop and they get discouraged, while the diet should be the priority.
For non-extreme naturals, bulk/cut becomes yo-yo dieting: gaining the same 20 lbs every bulk and cutting the same 15 every cut, with no progress, stressing metabolism and over-focusing on diet.
The '70% diet' saying from pro bodybuilding is false for naturals: diet isn't complicated, you don't need that many calories unless very big, and hitting macros is easy; training is what matters.
Cutting as a natural makes you feel awful and low-energy, so you don't put in the training work you should.
Use very small deficits or surpluses depending on goals, staying around maintenance most of the time.

Maintaining bodyweight doesn't mean maintaining muscle: bedridden at 190 lbs you could stay 190 but lose muscle; conversely you can stay at 200 lbs for three years while dropping fat and gaining muscle.
A calorie deficit makes building new muscle almost impossible, but a small surplus or maintenance works perfectly fine.
Men starting out who are not very over- or underweight should 'perma-bulk': stay in a small surplus continuously and keep grinding.
He went from 120 lbs to 190-200 lbs gradually without spikes and made his best gains then; bulking from 200 to 240 is when he put on the most fat.
